beats.say: Open like a friendly teacher, pointing at the car dashboard photo beside the board: its screen shows 3472. We are going to read and write big four-digit numbers like this one, and the secret is that every digit has a job depending on where it sits. Mention the colour code: blue thousands, green hundreds, pink tens, yellow ones. No questions: this is the explaining part.

lines.say: Today we're going to meet big numbers, with four digits. Look at the car's dashboard in the picture. The little screen says 3472, the number of kilometres the car has travelled, and it's on the board too. It looks like a jumble of digits, but it isn't. Every single digit has a job, and the job depends on where it is sitting.

lines.text: Each digit's job depends on its PLACE
lines.say: Once you know the places, you can read any big number, write it, and break it into pieces. I'll use colours: blue for thousands, green for hundreds, pink for tens and yellow for ones.

beats.say: Teach the four places right to left, using the number in the chart: 4507. Ones first, then tens, hundreds, thousands, marking the digits IN PLACE. Explain what each place means (ones are single things, tens are bundles of ten). Point out the 0 in the tens place as a teaser: we come back to it. The tutor does all the talking.

lines.say: Now let's put a number in the place value chart. This one is 4507. We always start from the right-hand end, with the ones.

Watch my chalk, and look at the chart. The 7 on the end is in the ones place, so yellow. Next to it the 0 is in the tens place, pink. We'll come back to that zero in a minute. Then the 5 is in the hundreds place, green. And the digit right at the front, the 4, is in the thousands place, blue.
Ones are just single things. Six ones is six.
Tens are bundles of ten. In 4507 there are no bundles of ten at all, so the tens place holds a zero.
Hundreds are bundles of a hundred, so five hundreds is five hundred.
And thousands are bundles of a thousand, so four thousands is four thousand.

beats.say: Expanded form: put the digits' values together, exactly as the picture does for 4567. Write 4567 = 4000 + 500 + 60 + 7 with the colours, then read the number aloud in words. Explain partitioning = breaking a number into its place-value parts. No questions.

lines.say: Now let's take a new number, 4567, and find what each digit is really worth, just like the picture. Four thousand, plus five hundred, plus sixty, plus seven. If you add them up you get back to 4567. Writing it like this is called expanded form.

lines.text: Partitioning = breaking a number into its place-value parts
lines.say: And breaking a number up into its parts like this has a name: partitioning. It's the same idea you may have met with two-digit numbers, just with more places.

lines.text: 4567 → four thousand, five hundred and sixty-seven
lines.say: To say the number out loud, we just read the parts in order: four thousand, five hundred and sixty-seven. Easy once you can see the parts.

beats.say: The zero placeholder. Compare 4040 with 440, as in the picture. Show that the zeros hold the hundreds and ones places open. Light, curious tone. No questions: the tutor shows it.

lines.say: Now here's a number with something sneaky in it: four thousand and forty, written 4040. Look at the picture. There's a 4 in the thousands and a 4 in the tens. What about the hundreds and the ones?

There are no hundreds at all, and no ones. Not one bundle of a hundred, not a single one. So there's a zero in the hundreds place and a zero in the ones place, and each zero is saying: nothing here, but keep this place open.

What if we forgot the zeros and wrote 4, 4, 0? That's four hundred and forty, a completely different and much smaller number. See in the picture how the first 4 slides along into the hundreds column? The zeros are placeholders, and they keep every other digit in the right seat.

beats.say: From words to digits. 'four thousand and forty' -> 4040, with the counters in the picture: four in thousands, four in tens, none in hundreds or ones. Teach it by filling the four places and putting a zero in any place the words skip. No questions.

lines.say: How do we go the other way, from words to digits? Take the words four thousand and forty. Here's my method: draw four boxes, for thousands, hundreds, tens and ones, and put counters in them like the picture.

Four thousand, so a 4 in the first box. The words never mention any hundreds, so that box gets a zero. Forty is four tens, so a 4 in the tens box. And the words never mention any ones, so the last box gets a zero. Together that's four thousand and forty, written 4040.

lines.text: Skipped place in the words = a 0 in the number
lines.say: So whenever the words skip a place, that place gets a zero. That's the whole trick.

beats.say: Do one TOGETHER, 6481. The tutor sets it up; the child answers each step. Each question is written on the board first. Praise the reasoning in a sentence.

lines.say: Now it's your turn to help me. Here's a new number, six thousand four hundred and eighty-one.

lines.text: The 4 is in the hundreds place
lines.say: Yes, the 4 is the hundreds digit.

ask.prompt: In 6481, which place is the digit 4 in?
ask.onMiss: Count the places from the right: ones, tens, hundreds. Which is the 4?

lines.say: Four hundreds is four hundred. That's the value of that 4.

ask.prompt: So what is the value of the 4 in 6481?
ask.onMiss: Ask: it is 4 bundles of what? How much is each bundle worth?

lines.say: Perfect, and that's the full expanded form: six thousand, four hundred, eighty and one.

ask.prompt: Now partition the whole number, 6481, into place-value parts.
ask.onMiss: Start from the left: what is the 6 worth? Then the 4, the 8 and the 1.

beats.say: The child works alone: 7052 in expanded form, then the number for 'nine thousand and sixty'. Hint only if stuck. Praise each step they do themselves.

board.text: Your turn: 7052 and a number from words

lines.say: Your turn to lead. Here's a number with a zero hiding in it: seven thousand and fifty-two.
Good, there are no hundreds, so we leave them out or write nought hundreds.

ask.prompt: Partition 7052 into place-value parts. Watch out for the zero.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what digit is in the hundreds place? What is zero hundreds worth?

lines.say: Nine in the thousands, nothing in the hundreds, six in the tens, nothing in the ones: 9060.

ask.prompt: Write this number in digits: nine thousand and sixty.
ask.onMiss: Draw four boxes: Th, H, T, O. The words skip a place or two: what goes there?

beats.say: Final check: compare the value of the same digit in two numbers (the 5 in 5,230 and 2,053) and have the child explain why the zero matters.

lines.say: One more, a good one. Two numbers, five thousand two hundred and thirty, and two thousand and fifty-three. Both have a 5 in them.

lines.text: In 5230 the 5 is worth 5000. In 2053 the 5 is worth 50.
lines.say: The same digit is worth very different amounts. In the first number the 5 is thousands, worth five thousand. In the second it's in the tens place, worth fifty.

ask.prompt: Is the 5 worth the same in both numbers? What is it worth in each?
ask.onMiss: Ask: which place is the 5 in, in each number?

lines.text: The zero keeps every digit in its place
lines.say: So why do we need zeros at all? Because they hold the places open, and a digit's value depends on its place.

ask.prompt: Why do we write the zero in 5308 and not just 538?
ask.lookFor: The zero is a placeholder: without it the digits shift places and the number changes.
ask.onMiss: Ask: what would happen to the 5, the 3 and the 8 if the zero were missing?
